title: Buyer beware in the quarterback portal
text:
Ever since the introduction of NIL, every offseason in college football feels like a high-stakes auction. Coaches chase proven production, fan bases track portal rankings like recruiting classes, and big names arrive on campus with massive expectations on them. When a quarterback puts his name in the portal, the assumption usually is they want a new system, a fresh start, a higher star rating, or a bigger paycheck. For one reason or another they transfer, and automatically assume their performance will reach a new level. 
Looking back at the top 15 qualifying quarterbacks from the 2025 transfer portal, that assumption sometimes faces a harsh reality. Using data from Sports Reference and 247Sports, I filtered for quarterbacks who actually played meaningful snaps rather than brief end-of-game appearances, then tracked how those 15 passers performed in 2024 compared to 2025, and whether portal hype actually translated into better play once they got to their new schools. I stuck with completed full-season numbers from 2024 and 2025 rather than mixing in 2026 stats, since the 2026 season is still underway and partial-season numbers wouldn’t be a fair comparison. 
The quickest way to cut through the offseason noise is to look at what happened on the field before and after the moves. In the chart below, each quarterback’s 2024 passer efficiency rating (red) connects to his 2025 rating (green), ordered from the biggest drop at the top to the biggest jump at the bottom. 


Code
library(tidyverse)

portal <- read_csv("data/portal_qbs_2025.csv")
pass24 <- read_csv("data/passing_2024.csv") |>
  mutate(player = gsub("*", "", Player, fixed = TRUE)) |>
  select(player, Rate) |>
  rename(rate_24 = Rate)
pass25 <- read_csv("data/passing_2025.csv") |>
  mutate(player = gsub("*", "", Player, fixed = TRUE)) |>
  select(player, Rate, Yds, TD, Int) |>
  rename(rate_25 = Rate, yds_25 = Yds, td_25 = TD, int_25 = Int)
qbs <- portal |>
  inner_join(pass24) |>
  inner_join(pass25)

qbs <- qbs |>
  mutate(diff = rate_25 - rate_24)

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = qbs,
    aes(
      y = reorder(player, diff), yend = player,
      x = rate_24, xend = rate_25
    ),
    color = "lightgrey",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = qbs,
    aes(y = player, x = rate_24, color = "2024"),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = qbs,
    aes(y = player, x = rate_25, color = "2025"),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "darkgreen")) +
  labs(
    title = "Big-name transfer quarterbacks didn't always pay off",
    subtitle = "If 2025 (green) is to the right of 2024 (red), the QB improved. If it's to the left, he regressed.",
    x = "Passer Efficiency Rating",
    y = "",
    caption = "Source: Sports Reference & 247Sports | By: Caleb Krueger"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot", 
  ggsave("image.png")
  )









The first thing that jumped off the screen is how few of these moves actually produced a clear step forward. Most of the top quarterbacks either stayed in a similar performance range or even played worse after changing jerseys. Even when a player arrived with a lot of hype, a new offense and a new locker room didn’t automatically turn him into a more efficient passer. 
If changing scenery doesn’t guarantee a leap on its own, what about how highly the quarterback was rated coming out of the portal? To test that, I plotted each quarterback’s 247Sports portal rating against his 2025 passer efficiency rating. 


Code
library(ggrepel)
set.seed(1234)

mendoza <- qbs |> filter(player == "Fernando Mendoza")
nico <- qbs |> filter(player == "Nico Iamaleava")

ggplot() +
  geom_smooth(
    data = qbs,
    aes(x = portal_rating, y = rate_25),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "black",
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = qbs,
    aes(x = portal_rating, y = rate_25),
    color = "grey",
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = mendoza,
    aes(x = portal_rating, y = rate_25),
    color = "#990000",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = nico,
    aes(x = portal_rating, y = rate_25),
    color = "#2774AE",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = qbs,
    aes(x = portal_rating, y = rate_25, label = player),
    size = 2.7
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.865, 0.985)) +
  labs(
    title = "Higher transfer ratings didn't guarantee better 2025 play",
    subtitle = "Portal ratings showed almost no link to 2025 efficiency,\nfrom Indiana's Fernando Mendoza (red) to UCLA's Nico Iamaleava (blue).",
    x = "247Sports Portal Rating",
    y = "2025 Passer Efficiency Rating",
    caption = "Source: Sports Reference & 247Sports | By: Caleb Krueger"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )









The trend line tells a pretty clear story: portal ratings had almost no meaningful link to how efficiently these quarterbacks played in 2025 (p-value of 0.678, adjusted R-squared of -0.062). High marks in the portal didn’t reliably separate the passers who thrived from the ones who struggled. 
Two names stood out immediately on either side of the story. Fernando Mendoza (in red) didn’t just perform better at Indiana—he turned a transfer move into a historic run that ended with him winning the Heisman Trophy and helping Indiana win the national championship. On the flip side, Nico Iamaleva (in blue) carried on of the highest portal ratings in the group after UCLA leaving Tennessee, yet his 2025 passer efficiency sat well below the mark you would expect with all the hype around his move. 
Passer efficiency gives you the big picture, but box-score numbers help show what those swings looked like across a full season. This table sorts all 15 quarterbacks by their year-over-year efficiency change, alongside their 2024 and 2025 schools and their 2025 passing yards, touchdowns, and interceptions. 


Code
library(gt)

qbs |>
  select(player, old_school, new_school, yds_25, td_25, int_25, diff) |>
  arrange(desc(diff)) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    player = "Quarterback",
    old_school = "2024 School",
    new_school = "2025 School",
    yds_25 = "2025 Yards",
    td_25 = "TD",
    int_25 = "INT",
    diff = "Rating Change"
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Most top transfer quarterbacks took a step back in 2025",
    subtitle = "A fresh start rarely paid off—just five of the top 15 qualifying portal quarterbacks posted a higher efficiency rating in 2025."
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("title")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("subtitle")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md("**By:** Caleb Krueger  |  **Source:** Sports Reference & 247Sports")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
    style = list(
      cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(3)),
      cell_text(weight = "bold", size = 12)
    )
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(yds_25),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(diff),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#990000"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(
      rows = player == "Fernando Mendoza"
    )
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#2774AE"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(
      rows = player == "Nico Iamaleava"
    )
  )

Only five of the 15 qualifying portal quarterbacks had a higher passer efficiency rating in 2025 than they had the year before. Mendoza led the improvers with 3,535 passing yards, 41 touchdowns, and just 6 interceptions on his way to a +38.3 efficiency jump, a Heisman Trophy winner, and eventually becoming the No.1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. Other Quarterbacks like Conner Weigman (+30.7), Devon Dampier (+25.2), and Carson Beck (+11.7; 3,813 yards, 30 TDS, 12 INTs at Miami before hearing his name called by the Cardinals in the 2026 NFL Draft) also turned their moves into big seasons. Meanwhile, the majority of the list, including high-profile transfers like Nico Iamaleava (-21.8) and John Matter (-34.7) saw their efficiency dip after switching teams, leaving them questioning their decisions. 
None of this means the transfer portal doesn’t matter or that talented quarterbacks can’t revitalize their careers or play their way into the NFL Draft. It just means that a big portal rating or a big announcement isn’t a finished product. Fit, supporting cast, play-calling, and adjusting to a new level of competition all play huge roles, and with two-thirds of these top transfers taking a step back in efficiency, there are plenty of reminders to look closer before buying into the hype.

title: West Coast Flash Meets the Blue-Collar Big Ten
text:
When Oregon, USC, Washington, and UCLA officially joined the Big Ten in 2024, the biggest question surrounding conference realignment was whether the high-scoring West Coast offenses could survive Midwest physicality. Known for elite quarterback play and high-level passing attacks in the Pac-12, all four programs faced a steep adjustment period against a league that’s historically defined by gritty defenses, ball control, and trench play. 
Because the 2026 college football season is still underway, making partial-season statistics uneven due to varying strength of schedule and games played, examining full-season data from 2023 through 2025 provides the best look at how the transition initially played out. 
During their final Pac-12 campaign in 2023, Oregon, USC, and Washington all ranked among the nation’s most explosive offenses, each averaging more than 36 points per game, while UCLA trailed the group at 26.5 points per contest. However, year one in the new conference immediately tested those high-scoring averages.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)   
library(gt)

pac12_23 <- read_csv("data/pac12_23.csv", skip = 1) |> mutate(Season = 2023)
b1g_24 <- read_csv("data/b1g_24.csv", skip = 1) |> mutate(Season = 2024)
b1g_25 <- read_csv("data/b1g_25.csv", skip = 1) |> mutate(Season = 2025)

west_coast_teams <- c("Oregon", "USC", "Washington", "UCLA")

wc_lines <- bind_rows(pac12_23, b1g_24, b1g_25) |>
  filter(School %in% west_coast_teams)

b1g_lines <- bind_rows(b1g_24, b1g_25)

oregon <- wc_lines |> filter(School == "Oregon")
usc <- wc_lines |> filter(School == "USC")
washington <- wc_lines |> filter(School == "Washington")
ucla <- wc_lines |> filter(School == "UCLA")

indiana_label <- b1g_lines |> filter(School == "Indiana" & Season == 2025)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = b1g_lines, aes(x = Season, y = Pts, group = School), color = "lightgrey") +
  geom_point(data = b1g_lines, aes(x = Season, y = Pts), color = "lightgrey", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 27.1, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_line(data = oregon, aes(x = Season, y = Pts, group = School), color = "#154733", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = oregon, aes(x = Season, y = Pts), color = "#154733", size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = usc, aes(x = Season, y = Pts, group = School), color = "#990000", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = usc, aes(x = Season, y = Pts), color = "#990000", size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = washington, aes(x = Season, y = Pts, group = School), color = "#4B2E83", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = washington, aes(x = Season, y = Pts), color = "#4B2E83", size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = ucla, aes(x = Season, y = Pts, group = School), color = "#2D68C4", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = ucla, aes(x = Season, y = Pts), color = "#2D68C4", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = oregon |> filter(Season == 2025), aes(x = Season + 0.05, y = Pts, label = School), color = "#154733", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = usc |> filter(Season == 2025), aes(x = Season + 0.05, y = Pts, label = School), color = "#990000", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = washington |> filter(Season == 2025), aes(x = Season + 0.05, y = Pts, label = School), color = "#4B2E83", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = ucla |> filter(Season == 2025), aes(x = Season + 0.05, y = Pts, label = School), color = "#2D68C4", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = indiana_label, aes(x = Season + 0.05, y = Pts, label = School), color = "darkgrey", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 2023.32, y = 28.3, label = "2024-25 B1G Avg (27.1)"), size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2023, 2024, 2025), limits = c(2022.9, 2025.45)) +
  labs(
    title = "Big Ten Defenses Immediately Slowed Down West Coast Offenses",
    subtitle = "Every former Pac-12 team saw its scoring dip in 2024 before Oregon, USC, and Washington bounced back in 2025.",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Points Per Game",
    caption = "Source: Sports Reference | By: Caleb Krueger"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot", 
    ggsave("image.png")
  )









Every single former Pac-12 program saw its scoring output drop in its 2024 Big Ten debut. Washington suffered the steepest decline after losing key starters and its coaching staff from its 2023 national championship runner-up roster, going down from 36.0 points per game in 2023 to 23.4 in 2024, well below the Big Ten’s two-year average of 27.1 points per game. Oregon and USC also lost roughly 10 points per game off their 2023 paces, while UCLA plummeted below 19 points per game. 
By year two in 2025, three of the four newcomers had fully adjusted to the conference’s hard-nosed defensive schemes. Oregon (36.8 PPG), USC (35.8 PPG), and Washington (34.1 PPG) all surged back near the top of the conference scoring leaderboard, trailing only Indiana. UCLA, on the other hand, remained stagnant at the bottom of the league at 18.4 points per game. 
Yet rebounding on the scoreboard did not automatically translate to conference supremacy. To understand why Oregon immediately emerged as an elite Big Ten contender while the other three programs fought for consistency over the first two seasons, you have to look at both sides of the ball. 


Code
b1g_24_ratings <- read_csv("data/b1g_24_ratings.csv", skip = 1)
b1g_25_ratings <- read_csv("data/b1g_25_ratings.csv", skip = 1)

b1g_combined <- bind_rows(b1g_24_ratings, b1g_25_ratings) |>
  group_by(School) |>
  summarise(
    Wins = sum(W),
    OSRS = mean(OSRS),
    DSRS = mean(DSRS),
    SRS = mean(SRS)
  )

oregon <- b1g_combined |> filter(School == "Oregon")
usc <- b1g_combined |> filter(School == "USC")
washington <- b1g_combined |> filter(School == "Washington")
ucla <- b1g_combined |> filter(School == "UCLA")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = b1g_combined, aes(x = DSRS, y = OSRS, size = Wins), color = "grey", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = ucla, aes(x = DSRS, y = OSRS), color = "#2D68C4", size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = usc, aes(x = DSRS, y = OSRS), color = "#990000", size = 4.2) +
  geom_point(data = washington, aes(x = DSRS, y = OSRS), color = "#4B2E83", size = 4) +
  geom_point(data = oregon, aes(x = DSRS, y = OSRS), color = "#154733", size = 6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 3.16, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5.38, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_text_repel(data = b1g_combined, aes(x = DSRS, y = OSRS, label = School), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 13.5, y = 12.5, label = "Good Defense, Good Offense"), size = 3, color = "blue") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.5, y = -5.5, label = "Bad Defense, Bad Offense"), size = 3, color = "blue") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 13.5, y = 3.85, label = "Big Ten Avg Offense"), size = 3, color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 3.2, y = 12.5, label = "Big Ten Avg Defense"), size = 3, color = "black") +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 6), name = "2-Yr Wins") +
  labs(
    title = "Defense Separated Oregon From Its West Coast Peers",
    subtitle = "Combined 2024–25 Big Ten averages. Oregon was the only newcomer with an above-average offense and defense.",
    x = "Defensive Rating",
    y = "Offensive Rating",
    caption = "Source: Sports Reference | By: Caleb Krueger"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )









Across the 2024 and 2025 seasons combined, Oregon was the only West Coast newcomer to have both an above-average Big Ten offense and an above-average defense. Landing firmly in the upper-right quadrant alongside conference heavyweights Ohio State, Indiana, and Penn State, the Ducks paired a top-tier offense rating with a lockdown defense to pile up the highest two-year win total among the four arrivals. 
USC proved its offensive scheme could still score at an elite level, boasting the second-highest offense rating among newcomers, but a below-average defense rating kept the Trojans out of the conference’s top team status. Washington hovered right above the Big Ten average line on both sides of the ball as it rebuilt its roster, while UCLA struggled in the bottom-left quadrant with one of the league’s least efficient offenses and defenses across 2024 and 2025.
While defenses separated the true contenders from the pack, a closer look at the offensive numbers reveals how West Coast style actually translated to the Midwest. 


Code
b1g_offense <- bind_rows(b1g_24, b1g_25) |>
  group_by(School) |>
  summarise(
    Pass_YPG = mean(`Yds...8`),
    Rush_YPG = mean(`Yds...11`),
    Total_YPG = mean(`Yds...15`)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(Total_YPG))

b1g_offense |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    School = "Team",
    Pass_YPG = "Pass YPG",
    Rush_YPG = "Rush YPG",
    Total_YPG = "Total YPG"
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Passing Traveled to the Big Ten — Rushing Didn't for All Four",
    subtitle = "Two-year offensive averages across 2024-25. Oregon and USC led the Big Ten in total yardage, while UCLA's ground game stalled."
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("title")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("subtitle")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md("**Source:** Sports Reference  |  **By:** Caleb Krueger")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
    style = list(
      cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(3)),
      cell_text(weight = "bold", size = 12)
    )
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Pass_YPG, Rush_YPG, Total_YPG),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#154733"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(rows = School == "Oregon")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#990000"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(rows = School == "USC")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#4B2E83"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(rows = School == "Washington")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "#2D68C4"),
      cell_text(color = "white")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(rows = School == "UCLA")

Even with the initial 2024 scoring dip, West Coast passing attacks didn’t just survive in the Big Ten, they out-passed the entire conference in yardage. Over the two-year span from 2024 to 2025, USC (451.4 total YPG) and Oregon (444.8 total YPG) led the Big Ten in total offense, with Washington (400.2 total YPG) also in the top five alongside Indiana and Ohio State. All three programs averaged more than 253 passing yards per game, proving that once they adjusted to their new surroundings, aerial attacks could still thrive against Big Ten secondaries. 
The difference between an elite offense and a stagnant one came down to balance in the run game. Oregon paired its 266.6 passing yards per game with a physical 178.2 rushing yards per game, giving the Ducks the ground presence required to wear down Big Ten fronts. USC (157.4 rush YPG) and Washington (147.2 rush YPG) also maintained reliable rushing averages to keep opposing defenses on their toes. 
Even UCLA proved its passing game could move the ball, averaging a respectable 211.2 passing yards per game, out-throwing better offenses such as Penn State (207.8 passing YPG), Michigan (157.9 passing YPG), and Iowa (137.4 passing YPG). However, the Bruins’ ground game stalled out completely at just 113.1 rushing yards per game, dragging their total offense down to 324.4 yards per contest and leaving them one-dimensional and toward the bottom of the league in scoring through 2025. 
Now past the midpoint of the 2026 season, the lessons from the first two seasons are playing out in dramatic fashion. While Oregon, USC, and Washington needed just one offseason in 2025 to adapt their offenses to Big Ten play, UCLA’s full roster and scheme overhaul simply took an extra year to materialize. After sitting in the bottom-left quadrant for two straight seasons, the Bruins have flipped the script in 2026, surging to an undefeated start (9-0 overall, 6-0 Big Ten) behind a revitalized offense and hard-nosed defense, including a statement 17-15 road win at Autzen Stadium over Oregon and a 34-20 road win at Minnesota this past weekend. 
Meanwhile, the other three newcomers are battling through the weekly grind of conference play. USC (7-2, 4-2 Big Ten) and Oregon (6-3, 4-2 Big Ten) sit in the upper tier of the conference standings behind high-powered, balanced attacks, with the Ducks bouncing back from a midseason offensive slump with a massive 41-28 road win at Ohio State this past Saturday. Washington (5-4, 2-4 Big Ten) remains in the middle of the pack after coming up just short in a 28-25 battle against Penn State. Ultimately, nearly three years of Big Ten expansion has proven that while West Coast passing can rack up yards anywhere, winning consistently in the Midwest requires a complete defense, a balanced rushing attack, and good trench play.
